interactions.label: A carrier of a Robertsonian translocation has only 45 chromosomes on counting, y

params.question: A carrier of a Robertsonian translocation has only 45 chromosomes on counting, yet is generally healthy. Which of the following best explains this finding?

answers.text: The missing chromosome contained only non-essential genes that are not required for normal development

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. All chromosomes carry essential genes. A truly missing chromosome would cause a monosomy, which is usually lethal. The carrier is healthy because no genetic material is actually absent.

answers.text: Two acrocentric chromosomes have fused at their centromeres into one large chromosome, so no genetic material is lost

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In a Robertsonian translocation, two acrocentric chromosomes (from groups 13, 14, 15, 21, 22) fuse at their centromeres, creating one combined chromosome. The count drops to 45 but all genetic material is preserved, which is why carriers are phenotypically normal.

answers.text: The remaining chromosomes compensate by increasing their gene expression to cover the missing material

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. There is no compensatory upregulation from other chromosomes. The carrier is healthy specifically because the fused chromosome retains all the genetic material from both original chromosomes — nothing is missing.

answers.text: The human body can function normally with any chromosome number between 44 and 48

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Chromosome number matters greatly in human biology. Most aneuploidies cause severe disease or are incompatible with life. The translocation carrier is healthy only because no genetic material has been lost despite the reduced count.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the concept of Robertsonian translocation. Two acrocentric chromosomes fuse at their centromeres to form one combined chromosome. The count drops to 45 but no genetic material is lost, which is why carriers are healthy. However, their offspring may inherit an unbalanced form.

Well done. In a Robertsonian translocation, two acrocentric chromosomes fuse at their centromeres. The total count drops to 45 but all genetic material is preserved — which is why carriers are healthy, even though their offspring may inherit an unbalanced form leading to trisomy.

interactions.label: Turner syndrome should only be suspected in girls who display classic features s

params.question: Turner syndrome should only be suspected in girls who display classic features such as a webbed neck and lymphoedema.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is actually false. Mosaic Turner syndrome can look completely typical, with none of the classic dysmorphic features. A high index of suspicion is essential — Turner syndrome should be considered in any girl with unexplained short stature, even if she appears otherwise healthy, to avoid missing the window for growth hormone therapy.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Mosaic Turner syndrome, where only some cells lack an X chromosome, can present without any classic features. The video stresses that Turner syndrome should be considered in any girl with unexplained short stature, because early diagnosis enables timely growth hormone therapy.

interactions.label: Down syndrome causes defects across multiple organ systems — heart, gut, immune

params.question: Down syndrome causes defects across multiple organ systems — heart, gut, immune system, and thyroid. Which of the following best explains why so many systems are affected simultaneously?

answers.text: Each complication is caused by a separate point mutation on chromosome 21

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Down syndrome is not caused by individual gene mutations. The problem is having an entire extra chromosome, which increases the dosage of approximately 300 genes at once, disrupting multiple developmental pathways.

answers.text: The extra copy of chromosome 21 increases the dosage of approximately 300 genes, disrupting developmental pathways across multiple organ systems

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Having three copies of chromosome 21 means roughly 300 genes are expressed at 1.5 times the normal level. This gene-dosage effect disrupts endocardial cushion formation (leading to cardiac septal defects), intestinal rotation (causing duodenal atresia), immune regulation (raising leukaemia risk), and thyroid function.

answers.text: These are coincidental findings that happen to be statistically more common in premature infants

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. These complications are directly caused by trisomy 21, not prematurity. They arise because the extra chromosome disrupts embryonic developmental pathways across multiple organ systems through the gene-dosage effect.

answers.text: The intellectual disability impairs autonomic nervous system regulation, which secondarily damages organ development

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The multi-system complications arise during embryonic development from gene-dosage effects, not from the intellectual disability. Cardiac defects and gut malformations form well before any neurological impact becomes clinically apparent.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key concept is gene-dosage effect. Having three copies of chromosome 21 (~300 genes at 1.5× normal dosage) disrupts developmental pathways across heart, gut, immune, thyroid, and other systems. This is why structured surveillance for these complications is the cornerstone of Down syndrome care.

Exactly right. The gene-dosage effect from three copies of chromosome 21 disrupts multiple developmental pathways simultaneously. This is why congenital heart disease (nearly 50% of cases), gut malformations, and other complications all trace back to the same underlying chromosomal cause.

interactions.label: The parents of a child newly diagnosed with Down syndrome ask what kind of care

params.question: The parents of a child newly diagnosed with Down syndrome ask what kind of care their child will need. Which of the following best describes the recommended management approach?

answers.text: The child should be managed primarily by a cardiologist, with other specialists consulted only if specific problems arise

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While cardiac screening is the top priority (congenital heart disease occurs in nearly half of cases), Down syndrome affects multiple organ systems. A paediatrician should coordinate input from cardiology, audiology, ophthalmology, physiotherapy, speech therapy, and other specialists.

answers.text: Routine developmental check-ups with the general practitioner are sufficient until school age

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Down syndrome requires proactive, specialised surveillance well beyond routine check-ups. Treatable complications such as cardiac defects, thyroid disease, hearing loss, and atlantoaxial instability need systematic screening at specific ages throughout childhood.

answers.text: A paediatrician should coordinate a multidisciplinary team following a structured surveillance schedule, with early intervention begun in infancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The paediatrician sits at the centre of a multidisciplinary network — coordinating cardiology, surgery, audiology, ophthalmology, physiotherapy, and speech therapy. Early intervention started in infancy, combined with inclusive education, produces far better cognitive and social outcomes than delayed or fragmented care.

answers.text: Specialised residential care should be arranged, as the child's complex needs cannot be adequately met at home

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The evidence-based approach has shifted decisively from custodial care to active inclusion and supported independence. Early intervention and inclusive schooling produce significantly better developmental outcomes than segregated care models.

overallFeedback.feedback: The recommended approach is paediatrician-coordinated multidisciplinary care with a structured surveillance schedule. Early intervention in infancy, combined with inclusive education and proactive screening for treatable complications, produces far better outcomes than reactive or segregated care.

Well done. Modern Down syndrome management centres on the paediatrician coordinating a multidisciplinary team with a structured surveillance schedule. Early intervention begun in infancy yields significantly better cognitive and social outcomes — the goal is active inclusion, not custodial management.

interactions.label: A karyotype report for a girl with Down syndrome reads '46,XX,der(14;21)'. A col

params.question: A karyotype report for a girl with Down syndrome reads '46,XX,der(14;21)'. A colleague suggests the result must be normal because the chromosome count is 46. Which of the following best explains why this reasoning is incorrect?

answers.text: Any karyotype with additional notation after the sex chromosomes is automatically abnormal regardless of the count

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While additional notation often indicates an abnormality, this answer does not explain the mechanism. The specific notation 'der(14;21)' means chromosomes 14 and 21 have fused, producing three functional copies of chromosome 21 material despite only 46 countable chromosomes.

answers.text: The 'der(14;21)' indicates a Robertsonian translocation in which chromosome 21 material is fused onto chromosome 14, giving three functional copies of chromosome 21 despite the normal count

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In translocation Down syndrome (~4% of cases), chromosome 21 is attached to chromosome 14, forming a derivative chromosome. The count reads 46, but there are effectively three copies of chromosome 21 genetic material — two free copies and one fused onto chromosome 14. Parent karyotyping is mandatory because a carrier parent faces a substantially higher recurrence risk than in free trisomy.

answers.text: The result indicates mosaicism, where some cells have 47 chromosomes and others have 46, producing a misleading average count

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This is not mosaicism. Mosaicism means different cell lines carry different chromosome complements. Here, 'der(14;21)' describes a Robertsonian translocation — a structural rearrangement in which chromosome 21 material is fused onto chromosome 14, present uniformly in all cells.

answers.text: The XX designation confirms Turner syndrome rather than Down syndrome, making the colleague's interpretation irrelevant

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. XX simply indicates a female karyotype. Turner syndrome involves a missing X chromosome (45,X). The der(14;21) in this report describes a structural rearrangement of chromosomes 14 and 21, confirming translocation Down syndrome.

overallFeedback.feedback: In translocation Down syndrome, chromosome 21 is fused onto another chromosome (typically 14), so the count reads 46 but there are three functional copies of chromosome 21 material. This is why careful karyotype interpretation is essential — and why parent karyotyping must follow to determine recurrence risk for future pregnancies.

Exactly right. Translocation Down syndrome can have a normal chromosome count of 46, which is why karyotype interpretation — not just chromosome counting — is essential. Identifying the translocation is clinically critical because parent karyotyping must follow to determine recurrence risk.
